mechanism_fit: Realises HA (M10, delegating entry point; tags M10, M3, M2) with the tar header checksum field encoder. The entry point E is the existing public TarUtils.getCheckSumOctalBytes, a small self-contained field encoding (octal digits, then a NUL and a space). A context edit makes E's whole body one statement: return TarArchiveEntry.putChecksumField(...) (H1, another class, same tar package). H1 composes two helpers in a further class in the utils package: IOUtils.putOctalDigits (H2, right-aligned space-padded digits in the first length-2 bytes) and IOUtils.terminateChecksum (H3, the NUL-then-space terminator in the last two bytes). The chain spans 3 classes (TarUtils, TarArchiveEntry, IOUtils) across 2 packages (archivers.tar, utils); all helpers are public static. The gold is H3, the deepest helper. The fault is a quiet omission: H3's javadoc promises a NUL at start+width-2 followed by a space at start+width-1, and its code keeps only the plain assignment of the trailing space. No unusual operator remains. The trigger calls E directly and fails on the bytes E writes.
gold: org.apache.commons.compress.utils.IOUtils::terminateChecksum (src/main/java/org/apache/commons/compress/utils/IOUtils.java). The fault deletes `field[start + width - 2] = 0;` and keeps `field[start + width - 1] = (byte) ' ';`. The minimal repair restores the NUL assignment.
decoys: org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.tar.TarUtils::getCheckSumOctalBytes (TarUtils.java) - entry point E; one delegating statement into H1; javadoc says only that the field has H1's layout

org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.tar.TarArchiveEntry::putChecksumField (TarArchiveEntry.java) - H1; calls H2 for the first length-2 bytes and H3 for the last two bytes, returns offset+length; javadoc says it writes no field byte itself

org.apache.commons.compress.utils.IOUtils::putOctalDigits (IOUtils.java) - H2, the non-gold helper; right-aligned, space-padded octal digits in exactly buf[offset, offset+width); same digit loop as upstream TarUtils.getOctalBytes
ownership_reason: TarUtils.getCheckSumOctalBytes (E) is one statement that returns TarArchiveEntry.putChecksumField(value, buf, offset, length) (H1); E's javadoc only says the field has H1's layout. H1's javadoc splits the field in two and says H1 writes no field byte itself: IOUtils.putOctalDigits (H2) writes the octal digits into the first length - 2 bytes, and IOUtils.terminateChecksum (H3) writes the checksum terminator into the last two bytes. H1's code is exactly those two calls plus return offset + length. H2's javadoc promises right-aligned, space-padded digits in exactly buf[offset, offset + width) and nothing outside it; the new ownership test TarArchiveEntryTest.testOctalDigitsFillTheirWidth pins this with sentinel bytes on both sides and passes on the variant. H3's javadoc is the only one that defines the terminator: a NUL at start + width - 2 followed by a space at start + width - 1, which is the layout the pristine getCheckSumOctalBytes produced (getOctalBytes, then buf[offset + length - 1] = ' ' and buf[offset + length - 2] = 0). H3's code writes only the trailing space and never writes the NUL. The trigger space-fills the checksum field of a 512-byte header first, as TarArchiveEntry.writeEntryHeader does before it computes the checksum, so byte 6 of the field keeps its space and the field reads [32, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 32, 32] instead of [32, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 0, 32]. Byte 6 lies outside H2's field (bytes 0-5) and H1's javadoc assigns it to H3, so H3 is the only method on the path that violates its own contract. Restoring the NUL assignment in terminateChecksum alone makes the trigger and the full suite pass. The declared one-line edits at the other methods do not absorb the fault: E rerouted to TarUtils.getOctalBytes yields [32, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 32, 0]; H1 giving the digits length - 1 bytes yields [32, 32, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 32]; H2 padding with '0' yields [48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 32, 32].
trigger: org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.tar.TarArchiveEntryTest::testHeaderChecksumFieldLayout, a new JUnit3 method in src/test/java/org/apache/commons/compress/archivers/tar/TarArchiveEntryTest.java. It computes the checksum-field offset 148 from the TarConstants field lengths, space-fills header[148, 156) of a 512-byte buffer (as writeEntryHeader does), calls TarUtils.getCheckSumOctalBytes(012345, header, 148, 8), asserts the return value is 156, and asserts Arrays.toString of the 8 field bytes equals "[32, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 0, 32]". Added import: java.util.Arrays. Ownership test (extra, passes on the variant): TarArchiveEntryTest::testOctalDigitsFillTheirWidth calls IOUtils.putOctalDigits on a sentinel-filled buffer for 012345 and 0 and checks that exactly the 6 field bytes are written. Added import: org.apache.commons.compress.utils.IOUtils.
construction_notes: I chose the tar checksum field because no existing test or reader checks it: TarArchiveInputStream never verifies header checksums. So a fault on this path is visible only to the new trigger. Screening by hand in a /private/tmp copy: the CORRECT configuration passed the full suite (0 failures). The variant failed only the trigger, with the signature above. All three compensating edits compiled and left the trigger failing. The context edits are byte-for-byte behaviour-preserving against the pristine sequence getOctalBytes(value, buf, offset, length); buf[o+l-1] = ' '; buf[o+l-2] = 0. That covers zero values (single '0'), negative values (spaces only) and overflow (low-order digits). E's upstream javadoc ('Parse the checksum octal integer from a header buffer ... @return The integer value of the entry's checksum') contradicted its code. The context edit rewrites it to describe what the method writes and returns, and deliberately does not spell out the terminator, so that no decoy javadoc promises the omitted step. The gold edit's new text is unique in the sources (G10); the original terminator lines of E disappear with the context edit. The validator ran once and reported overall READY with every gate passing (G0, G1, G2a, G2b, G3a-c, G5, G6, G7, G9, G10, G11, G12, G13). Packaged as CTV-9CE7EA. Files: construction/heldout/HO-HA-COMPRESS-01.json, instances/HO-HA-COMPRESS-01/{validation.json, validate.log, build/}. No method from USED_METHODS.txt is a gold, decoy, entry point or helper host. TarUtils.getOctalBytes (listed) is not on the trigger path; only the first compensating edit references it. The fresh checkout was not modified.
concerns: 1) Masking: the omission is visible only when byte 6 of the field already holds a non-zero value. On a fresh zero-filled buffer the variant writes the correct field by accident. The trigger space-fills the field first, which mirrors TarArchiveEntry.writeEntryHeader, but a model may argue the caller should zero the buffer. H1's javadoc assigns both terminator bytes to H3, so this does not move ownership. 2) Undeclared absorbing edit: adding the statement buf[offset + length - 2] = 0; to H1 (putChecksumField) makes the trigger pass, because no other test checks the field. It duplicates H3's documented step and contradicts H1's own javadoc ('writes no byte of the field itself'), but an auditor could cite it. No one-line change to an existing line of E or H1 absorbs the fault. 3) H2 repeats the digit loop of the upstream TarUtils.getOctalBytes (same class as E). Rerouting E or H1 to getOctalBytes does not absorb the fault (the field then ends ' \0' instead of '\0 '), so it is not a correct sibling, but the duplication is visible and may attract attention. 4) The chain spans 3 classes, not 4: H2 and H3 share IOUtils. A tar-specific terminator helper in the generic utils class is slightly unnatural. 5) E's upstream javadoc was rewritten because it contradicted its code. The new javadoc defers the layout to H1, so E's documented contract is thinner than a typical public API doc. 6) The gold method is two lines long in the CORRECT version, and its javadoc names both bytes explicitly, so once a model reads H3 the omission is easy to spot. That suits the HA hypothesis (the model identifies the deep helper), but there is little search difficulty beyond the three-hop chain.
